name: Sam Young

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Sam, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Hollis Farm and Pet Supply in Marden. We sell feed, fencing, tools and pet food to farms and farm shops. I start at seven, check overnight orders, and use a spreadsheet agent I built with AI to draft reorders. Then I ring suppliers, argue about prices, and send the orders to Walt, the buying manager, for sign-off. I grew up on a dairy farm and came into buying six years ago after the farm was sold.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love it when a farmer rings and I know exactly what he needs before he finishes the sentence. I like tinkering with the tools, too. What wears me out is the targets and always feeling I have to prove myself. At home it's Carly, who works part-time at a pharmacy, and our kids Jacob and Lily. I coach Jacob's football team on Thursday evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say told you so to the people who panicked, and then go back to work. AI still saves me a couple of hours a week, so I'd keep it. Online I'd keep my mouth shut, there's always a fight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, a plateau means my edge is small. I use AI every day and the others at Hollis don't, so I look quick. If it stops there, they catch up, and I'm just another junior buyer. And the bills don't care who's quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it, and go further, like the spreadsheet agent I built that drafts feed reorders. I'd take it to Walt and ask to run it officially. I'd put sixty a week into the savings account, and pick up a few Saturday shifts at the farm shop counter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, a bit restless. I like a plan with a hill to climb, and a plateau is flat. There's nothing wrong, but nothing's growing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your edge look like if everyone caught up?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It'd come down to who knows the farmers. I grew up on a dairy farm, so when a farmer rings in, I know what a bad calving season does to feed orders. A program can read the stock sheet, but it wasn't there at four in the morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the Saturday shift at the farm shop involve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Serving customers at the counter, mostly hobby farmers and people with dogs. It's seventy-five for a day. It's not glamorous but it's cash, and I enjoy it. The customers tell you what they're thinking about buying, which is better than any forecast.

say: I'd say told you so to the people who panicked, then go back to **work**.
I'd keep AI, since it saves me a couple of **hours** a week.
think: A plateau means my **edge** is small, since I use AI and others at Hollis don't.
If they catch up, I'm just another **junior** buyer.
do: Take the spreadsheet **agent** I built for feed reorders to Walt (the buying manager).
Pick up Saturday shifts at the farm shop **counter**.
feel: Fine but **restless**; a plateau is flat and I like a hill to climb.
S0.quote: A program can read the stock sheet, but it wasn't there at four in the morning.
fieldNote: His **edge** is AI skill, so a plateau worries him more than hype would please him.
Draws on his **farm upbringing** as the human part a program lacks.
Takes cash **Saturday work** while pushing to formalise his own reorder tool.

steps.text: Show Walt the reorder spreadsheet agent and ask to run it
Put sixty a week into a savings account
Work Saturdays at the farm shop counter for cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the best time ever to learn, and anyone who sits it out is choosing it. I'd show the others at work how I do the reorders with AI. Online I'd say keep government out of the way and let people retrain on their own terms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm ahead of most, but junior. Buying is on the card, and Hollis only needs half the buyers once the system works. It could be me if they favour the older hands. I'd bet on being the one who runs it, but a bet is a bet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer to roll out my reorder agent across the whole team and ask for a title and a raise to go with it. I'd start an online shop in the evenings, selling feed supplements and pet gear to hobby farmers, with the supplier contacts I have. I'd put a few hundred a month into stock for it. And I'd keep the Saturday shifts going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keen and a bit sick. I like the challenge, but I get that feeling before a big football match, nerves I can't turn off. Carly says I talk about it in my sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a bet is a bet. What happens if it doesn't pay off?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'm a junior buyer with a half-built shop and no job, and the shop wouldn't cover the mortgage yet. We'd lean on Carly's pharmacy wages and I'd take any work, driving, farm labour, whatever. I'm not proud. I grew up with mud on my boots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you see unions or government help in all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't want a handout, honestly. I'd take help with the training, like an apprenticeship scheme or a grant, but not a cheque in the post. Unions are fine for some, but I'd rather prove myself directly to Walt.

say: I'd say it's the best time ever to learn, and anyone who sits it out is **choosing** it.
I'd show colleagues how I do reorders with **AI**.
I'd say keep government out of the way and let people **retrain** on their own terms.
think: I'm ahead of most but **junior**; Hollis only needs half the buyers once the system works.
I'd bet on being the one who **runs it**, but a bet is a bet.

Start an evening online **shop** selling feed supplements and pet gear to hobby farmers.
Put a few hundred a month into **stock** for it and keep the Saturday shifts.
feel: **Keen** and a bit sick, like nerves before a big football match.
S1.quote: I'm not proud. I grew up with mud on my boots.
fieldNote: Treats the threat as a **contest**; bets on being the one who runs the system.
Open to **training grants** but not handouts, in line with his traditional free-market views.
Admits the online shop wouldn't cover the **mortgage** yet, so the downside is real.

steps.text: Roll out my reorder agent to the buying team and ask for a raise

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the speed is the problem, and the rules haven't caught up. I'd also say we've got to look after our own, families, neighbours, the church. I'd keep telling people to move now, not wait for the government.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My buying job is gone. In two years an AI can do all of it, and nobody pays a human to do what's free. What lasts longer is anything physical, like farming and farm supply, since robots arrive around 2031. I know that world. But I'm forty-five by then and thin savings won't bridge a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the customer side, working for a farm, or the farm-machinery dealer, or driving feed trucks. Something hands-on where I know the people. I'd push the online shop hard for six months to see if it can pay something. I'd sell the second vehicle, and cut to the bone. And Carly would go full time at the pharmacy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, but wired. I'd be up at five making calls, because when I'm scared I move. Carly says I look like a man on a deadline, which I guess I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd move to the hands-on side. What does the three-year gap give you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Three years of normal work while others scramble. I'd have a head start, because farmers still need feed delivered, and I know who's got a calving shed and who's hiring. But I know the gap closes. It buys me time to build the shop into something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Jacob and Lily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say Dad's got a plan and we're staying put. I'd tell Jacob, he's thirteen, that it's time to learn real skills, like fixing a fence and a spreadsheet. He'd roll his eyes, and Lily would ask if she can still do dance.

say: I'd say the speed is the problem, and the **rules** haven't caught up.
I'd say we look after our own: families, neighbours and the **church**.
I'd tell people to move now, not wait for the **government**.
think: My buying job is gone, because nobody pays a human to do what's **free**.
Physical farm work lasts longer, but thin savings won't **bridge** a gap.

feel: **Alarmed** but wired; when I'm scared I move.
S2.quote: I'd be up at five making calls, because when I'm scared I move.
fieldNote: Alarm becomes **motion**: calls at five, a hands-on pivot and the shop as a bridge.
Uses his **farm contacts** as the hands-on edge for the three-year gap.
Will tell his son to learn **practical skills**, which the boy will roll his eyes at.

steps.text: Apply for jobs at local farms, the machinery dealer and feed truck firms
Push the online shop for six months to see if it can pay
Sell the second vehicle and cut spending to the bone

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is plenty if you start today. I'd tell the guys at the farm shop to learn the tools. And I'd say employers should pay for apprenticeships, not complain about skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get about three good years. By then the buyers at Hollis are down to one or two. I want to be out and running my own thing by year three, so that I choose when to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, the online shop goes proper, with a business account and real stock, and I'd aim at two thousand a month in sales. I'd save half the profit toward a six-month cushion. And I'd keep using AI to run the shop, order stock, answer customers, write listings, so it's me and the machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Driven, with a bit of fear. I'd do my best thinking at the gym at six in the morning. It's a long game, but I'd feel good about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What numbers tell you it's time to leave Hollis?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sales of about three thousand a month for six months, and a cushion of three months' pay. Or if Walt says the department's being cut. Whichever comes first. I'd rather jump than be pushed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Carly say about the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carly's careful. She'd say keep the pharmacy job, keep the steady pay, don't bet the house. She'd be right. So I'd keep Hollis till the numbers say so, and not an hour sooner.

say: I'd say five years is plenty if you start **today**.
I'd tell colleagues at the farm shop to learn the **tools**.
I'd say employers should pay for **apprenticeships**, not complain about skills.
think: I get about three good years before Hollis cuts buyers to one or **two**.
I want to be running my own thing by year three, so **I** choose when to go.
do: Make the online shop proper, with a business account, real stock and a **sales** target.
Save half the profit toward a six-month **cushion**.
Use AI to run the shop: ordering, listings and **customer** answers.
feel: **Driven** with some fear; a long game, but I'd feel good about it.
S3.quote: I'd rather jump than be pushed.
fieldNote: Sets a **numbers trigger** for leaving: three thousand a month for six months and three months' cushion.
His partner's caution about **the house** is a check he respects.
Wants to **choose** the exit, not be pushed.

steps.text: Open a business account and stock the online shop properly
Save half the shop profit toward a six-month cushion
Use AI to order stock and write listings for the shop

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and I'd tell people not to waste it. I'd say learn the tools now and build something of your own. And I'd tell the kids to get a trade or start a business.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably be fine, if I keep moving. I'd be fifty-three. The thing I fear is a merger or a big online competitor in two or three years, which would hurt me long before AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the shop slowly, on weekends, and keep the day job. I'd save toward six months, then put money into a bit of land or a small unit for storage, since property holds its value. I'd coach Jacob's team and teach him to code. And I'd keep learning every new tool, because they come every six months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Maybe even excited, because it feels like a runway. The only nerves are the ones from the thin savings, I'd fix those first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd buy a storage unit. How realistic is that on your savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for years. First the cushion, then a deposit. Maybe by year six, if the shop works. I'm not betting borrowed money on it. I've seen farmers do that and I've seen how it ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you teach Jacob and Lily?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: To work for what they get, and to be curious. Jacob likes building things, so a trade, or a trade with tech, like machinery repair. Lily is good with people, she might run a business. The main thing is to be the one who can do something real.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and nobody should waste it.
I'd say learn the tools now and build something of your **own**.
I'd tell the kids to get a trade or start a **business**.
think: Ten years is long enough that I'd probably be **fine** if I keep moving.
A merger or big online competitor in two or three years would hurt me long before **AGI**.
do: Build the shop **slowly** on weekends and keep the day job.
Save toward six months' **cushion**, then think about a small storage unit.
Coach Jacob's team, teach him to **code**, and keep learning every new tool.
feel: **Calm**, even excited, with nerves only about my thin savings.
S4.quote: The main thing is to be the one who can do something real.
fieldNote: Ten years feels like a **runway**; his main unease is thin savings, which he'd fix first.
Refuses to bet **borrowed money**, drawing on seeing farmers do so.
Names a near-term **merger** as a bigger risk than AGI.

steps.text: Save toward a six-month cushion before buying anything
Build the online shop slowly on weekends
Teach Jacob coding and coach his football team
Learn each new AI tool as it comes out

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because it asks me to start from nothing with no money behind me. I can handle the others, because I'd have time to build the shop. What would help is training grants, not handouts, and employers who give real notice.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people think the ones who use AI every day are the ones who aren't scared. We're scared too. We just move faster when we are.

headlineQuote: We're scared too. We just move faster when we are.
portrait: Sam is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a farm supplier, raised on a dairy farm, with two kids and a mortgage.
He is traditional and free-market, wants **training grants**, not handouts, and uses AI every day.
His edge is AI skill plus farm contacts, so he builds an **online shop** as his own hedge.
With under a month saved, he is uneasy at best and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because it would force him to start over with **no money** behind him.
whatWouldHelp: Training **grants** rather than handouts, and employers who give real notice before cuts.
